Text: The pelvic girdle mixes axial and appendicular bones: its posterior wall is the {{c1::sacrum and coccyx}} (axial), and its sides and front are the {{c2::two os coxae}} (appendicular).

Text: The {{c1::inguinal ligament}} stretches from the ASIS to the pubis.

Text: The ischial tuberosity (the manual's 'ischial ramus') can be felt by pressing hard on the buttocks at the level of the {{c1::gluteal fold}}.
Back Extra:
Why: the tuberosity lies deep to the lower buttock near the gluteal fold, so firm pressure with the gluteal muscles relaxed reaches the bone.

Pitfall: the manual and study guide call this bump the ischial ramus; the bone you press on through the buttock, and sit on, is the ischial tuberosity.

Text: The lab manual says the gluteal region belongs anatomically to the {{c1::trunk}} and physiologically to the {{c1::lower limb}}.
Back Extra:
Why: the gluteal region lies over the pelvis, but its muscles (the glutes) move the thigh.

Pitfall: most anatomy texts count the gluteal region as a region of the lower limb, the transition between trunk and thigh.

Text: A hip bone seen from its outer (lateral) side: is it a right or a left os coxae? {{c1::left::side}}

Why: crest up, obturator foramen down, acetabulum facing you (lateral view). The sciatic notches mark the back and sit on the picture's right, so the front (ASIS) points to your left: that is a left hip bone seen from outside.

Cue: Dr. Blais's recipe: crest superior, obturator foramen inferior, acetabulum lateral, sciatic notches posterior.
